Market attractiveness: moderate in theory, unproven in practice. The macro tailwinds are real (e-commerce growth, package theft, dense multi-family housing), and the underserved-neighborhood angle is a legitimate wedge since big locker operators prioritize higher-income buildings. But the plan offers no bottom-up sizing. 'Tens of thousands of shops' and 'billions in potential' are unsupported top-down claims. At the stated economics (~$1 per pickup, shop keeps ~40%, leaving ~$0.60), a locker needs roughly 100+ pickups a month just to produce ~$60 of gross revenue against hardware, cellular, insurance, and servicing costs. Unit economics likely look thin or negative unless volume per locker is high, and the plan admits payback is unknown. The real market is not 'apartment dwellers' but the subset who shop online frequently, lack secure delivery, live within walking distance of a participating shop, and will adopt a custom address code. That serviceable market is far smaller than implied, and low-income households have lower online order frequency, which pressures per-locker volume.

Target group: the segment is defensible but double-edged. Targeting overlooked neighborhoods differentiates the company and fits a real pain point, and the CEO's corner-store background helps with supply-side trust. However, the customer being served (price-sensitive residents) has the least willingness to pay per pickup or subscribe, and the plan's more credible revenue sources (carriers, retailers, property managers) are untested and not validated with any conversation or LOI. The buyer, user, and host are three different parties with distinct incentives, and only the shop side has any evidence. Fragmented small-shop hosts also create heavy acquisition and servicing overhead per location. The pivot to carriers and property managers could be the actual business, but that moves the company into direct competition with well-capitalized incumbents (Amazon, UPS, Package Concierge-type players), which contradicts the 'big companies ignore us' premise.

Scalability: the geographic model (neighborhood by neighborhood, city by city) is repeatable, and cellular-connected locks avoid per-site IT friction. But growth is capital-intensive because the company owns every unit, and density is required in each neighborhood to build habit and justify a route. The moat claim (local relationships) is weak: shop agreements are likely non-exclusive, hardware is replicable, and a carrier or large locker operator could copy the model once demand is proven. Network effects are minimal since each locker serves a small radius. The one real defensibility lever would be exclusive multi-year host contracts and carrier integration, neither of which exists yet.

Exit potential: limited and acquirer-dependent. Venture-scale outcomes look unlikely given thin per-unit margins, owned-hardware capex, and modest ARPU. The most plausible exits are an acqui-hire or asset/network acquisition by a carrier, locker operator, or last-mile logistics company seeking low-income urban coverage, likely at modest valuations. A stronger exit story would require evidence of high per-locker utilization, signed carrier or property-manager revenue, and exclusive shop contracts. Alternatively, it may fit better as a profitable, capital-light regional business or a mission-driven/community infrastructure model rather than a high-growth venture.

Bottom line: the market need is real and the niche is sensible, but the market is not yet shown to be large enough or monetizable enough to support scaling or a strong exit. Priority next steps are bottom-up sizing, per-locker utilization and payback data from several sites, and one or two paying carrier or property-manager commitments.

Business plan text:

Pawnshop Lockers
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Pawnshop Lockers
Submitted to the University Business Plan Competition
OVERVIEW
Pawnshop Lockers is a early stage Internet and Consumer Technology company that is building a
network of smart-lock parcel lockers placed inside corner stores and laundromats in apartment
heavy neighborhoods. Our mission is to be the trusted last step for packages in places where
the traditional delivery model is broken. We combine electronic hardware, a mobile app, and
local business partnerships into one solution that we believe is disruptive and scalable.
THE PROBLEM
Package theft is a huge problem in the United States. Millions of packages are stolen every
year according to various surveys we have read, and the problem is especially bad in dense
apartment neighborhoods where buildings dont have a doorman, a secure mailroom, or even a
working front door lock. Packages get left in hallways, on stoops, or in lobbies where anyone
can take them. Residents in these neighborhoods often work long or irregular hours so they cant
be home to receive deliveries. When a package is stolen the customer has to deal with the
retailer, wait for a replacement, and lose trust in online shopping. Several of our team
members have personally had packages stolen in the apartments they lived in while at school,
which is how we got the idea.
Existing solutions like the lockers in big chain stores and in some apartment lobbies are not
available in the neighborhoods that need them most, because those neighborhoods have older
buildings and lower income residents and are not a priority for large companies.
OUR SOLUTION
We install a modular locker unit inside a local corner store or laundromat. The unit has a
cellular connected smart lock on each compartment, so it doesnt need the shops wifi. A resident
signs up on our app, gets a Pawnshop Lockers address code, and uses it at checkout so their
package is sent to the locker. When it arrives, the resident receives a notification and a one
time pickup code. They walk to the shop, enter the code, and the door opens. The shop owner
does not have to handle any packages, which keeps their workload low, and they earn a fee each
time a package is picked up.
The name comes from the idea that the neighborhood shop is a trusted place that people already
visit, like a pawnshop used to be a neighborhood anchor. We think this brand is memorable.
THE MARKET
There are many apartment dwellers in America, and e-commerce keeps growing every year. If even
a small percent of these households used a locker near them, the market would be very large. We
estimate that there are tens of thousands of corner stores and laundromats in the target type
of neighborhood nationwide, and if each had a locker at a modest fee the revenue potential is
in the billions. Our initial target is a few neighborhoods in our city, then other cities with
similar density. We have not yet done a formal market sizing but we believe the top down
numbers are very promising.
BUSINESS MODEL
We make money in a few ways. First, we charge a fee per package pickup, part of which is passed
to the shop owner as their commission. Second, we plan to charge residents a small optional
subscription for extended storage time and text alerts. Third, we plan to partner with delivery
carriers and retailers who would pay us to use the lockers as a delivery destination, and with

property managers who would pay to offer the service to their tenants. The shop owner pays
nothing up front for the locker, as we cover the hardware cost and own the unit.
Our current pricing is around a dollar a pickup with the shop owner keeping roughly forty
percent, though this is still being tested. We expect the hardware to pay for itself over time
as volume grows, but we dont have enough data yet to say how long that will take.
COMPETITION
The space is crowded. There are large national locker companies, carrier owned lockers, retail
partnership pickup points, and apartment lobby locker systems. There are also package concierge
apps and neighborhood pickup point networks that use shops to hold packages by hand. We think
our difference is the focus on underserved neighborhoods, the use of smart lock hardware so
shop owners do not need to watch packages, and the fee model that gives shops a reason to
participate. We know bigger players could copy us, but we think our local relationships and
focus will be a moat.
THE TEAM
Devontae Ricks is the CEO and handles business development, shop relationships, and
fundraising. He studies business at our university and previously worked part time at a corner
store owned by his uncle, so he understands the shop owner side.
Marisol Quenneville is the CTO and leads the app and the electronics. She is a computer
engineering major and built our first working prototype of the locker door and lock controller.
Tobias Wangari-Holt is in charge of operations and design. He studies industrial design and is
responsible for the physical unit, installation, and the customer experience.
We also have informal advisors from our university, though we have not signed any formal
agreements with them.
MILESTONES AND FINANCIALS
We have registered the company, although the legal entity is not formed yet and we are working
on that step. We have a website. We built a working prototype and installed a first unit in one
laundromat near campus, and our first client has paid us. We have a small number of residents
signed up and a handful of packages have gone through the locker so far. Early feedback has
been positive, though the sample is small.
Our costs so far are mostly the hardware parts, the cellular service, and some small expenses
paid by the founders out of pocket. Revenue to date is very small, just the first payment and a
few pickup fees. We project that with additional lockers we could reach breakeven in a
reasonable time, and we expect revenue to grow quickly once we sign more shops, but we have not
finished a detailed financial model.
WHAT WE ARE ASKING FOR
We are applying to this competition for prize funding to build more locker units and install
them in additional shops, which we think will let us prove the model with real numbers. We
would use funds for hardware manufacturing, cellular and software costs, legal setup of the
company, and some marketing in the target neighborhoods. We would also value mentorship from
judges and experienced entrepreneurs about hardware, pricing, and how to approach carriers and
property managers. Finally, we are looking for introductions to local business associations
that could help us reach more shop owners.
CONCLUSION
Pawnshop Lockers has the potential to make package delivery safer and more convenient in
neighborhoods that big companies overlook, while giving local shops a new source of income. We

are passionate, hardworking, and excited to learn, and we believe this competition is the right
next step for us.

Question: Share thoughts on market attractiveness and exit potential. Address whether the market would support this venture, whether the company targets the correct group, and whether the market is large enough to support scaling.
